title: Docker Images & Layers
summary: The anatomy of a Docker image and how layer caching turns a slow build into a fast one.

slides.markdown:
A Docker image isn't one big blob — it's a stack of **layers**, each one a diff from the layer below, plus a small manifest describing how they fit together.

Think of it like a photo edit history: each layer is one edit (crop, filter, text), stored separately, and the final image is just all of them stacked in order. That's also exactly what makes builds fast: an unchanged early edit doesn't need to be redone.

slides.subTitle: Layers, manifest, config
slides.markdown:
An image is made of three parts: the **layers** themselves (each a tarball of filesystem changes, content-addressed by a hash), the **manifest** (lists which layers make up this image and in what order), and the **config** (metadata — the default command, environment variables, exposed ports, the entrypoint).

When you `docker pull`, you're really downloading the manifest, then fetching only the layers you don't already have locally — which is why pulling an updated image is often fast if most layers are unchanged.

slides.subTitle: How layers stack into one view
slides.markdown:
Every layer is read-only; the union filesystem overlays them so the running container sees one merged filesystem.

![How image layers stack into one merged filesystem view](assets/image-layer-stack.svg)

When a file exists in multiple layers, the **topmost** layer's version wins — this is how a later instruction can overwrite a file from an earlier one without physically deleting anything from the layers below.

assets.alt: How image layers stack into one merged filesystem view

slides.subTitle: The layer each one creates
slides.markdown:
Most Dockerfile instructions that touch the filesystem — `RUN`, `COPY`, `ADD` — each create a **new layer**. Metadata-only instructions like `ENV`, `EXPOSE`, and `CMD` update the image config instead, without adding a filesystem layer.

This is why a Dockerfile with ten `RUN apt-get install X` lines produces ten separate layers, each one storing only the files that specific command added or changed — not the layers before it.

slides.subTitle: Why instruction order changes build speed
slides.markdown:
Docker caches each layer and reuses it on the next build **if the instruction and its inputs are unchanged** — but the moment one layer's cache misses, every layer after it must rebuild too, even if they'd have produced identical output.

That's why you put rarely-changing instructions (installing OS packages, dependency installs) *before* frequently-changing ones (copying your app's source code) — a source change then only invalidates the last layer or two, not the expensive dependency install.

slides.subTitle: Mutable pointer vs content hash
slides.markdown:
| | Tag (e.g. `myapp:1.4`) | Digest (e.g. `myapp@sha256:ab12...`) |
|---|---|---|
| What it is | A human-readable, mutable label | A content hash of the exact image |
| Can change over time? | Yes — a tag can be repointed to a new image | No — the digest changes if the image content changes |
| Use for | Human-friendly versioning | Guaranteeing you deployed exactly this build |

**How to decide:** use tags for readability in day-to-day work, but pin deployments to a **digest** (or at minimum an immutable version tag) wherever reproducibility genuinely matters.

slides.subTitle: Reading `docker history`
slides.markdown:
`docker history myapp:1.4` lists every layer, its size, and the instruction that created it:

```
IMAGE          CREATED BY                          SIZE
a1b2c3d4       CMD ["node" "server.js"]            0B
e5f6a7b8       COPY . .                            2.1MB
c9d0e1f2       RUN npm install                     48MB
f3a4b5c6       COPY package.json .                 1.2KB
1a2b3c4d       FROM node:18-slim                   180MB
```

Reading bottom to top: the base image is 180MB, `npm install` adds 48MB, and the actual app code is a tiny 2.1MB — a common shape where dependencies dwarf the code you actually wrote.

**Wrong belief:** "I'll just push everything as `:latest` — it's simpler."

**Why it's wrong:** `:latest` is a mutable pointer that gets silently repointed on every push, so "deploy `:latest`" means something different every time. You lose the ability to know exactly what's running, roll back to a known-good version, or reproduce a bug against the image that caused it.

**Correct model:** tag every build with something immutable — a commit SHA or semver — and reserve `:latest`, if used at all, as a convenience alias, never what you actually deploy.

slides.subTitle: The push/pull flow
slides.markdown:
A **registry** stores images and serves them by tag or digest. `docker push` uploads any layers the registry doesn't already have plus the manifest; `docker pull` does the reverse. Public registries (Docker Hub) host open-source images; private registries (a cloud provider's container registry, or a self-hosted one) hold your proprietary images behind authentication.

Most CI pipelines end with a push to a private registry, and most deployments start with a pull from it — the registry is the handoff point between building and running.
